newsitem.title: DENMARK: Danish bankers say EMU opt-out could help bonds.
newsitem.headline: Danish bankers say EMU opt-out could help bonds.

text.p: Executives of Denmark's two biggest banks on Monday said Denmark's decision not to join European Economic and Monetary Union could have a beneficial effect on Danish bonds.

Analysts say that Denmark's 1993 opt-out from EMU has added between 0.5 and 1.0 percentage point to benchmark bond yields but Den Danske Bank's Mads Jacobsen believes that will change if other EU members implement the planned common currency,the Euro.
"My expectation is that one will see the Euro as generally a little weaker than the present mark," Jacobsen told the Danish daily Berlingske Tidende.
"Therefore I believe that the gap between the Danish crown and interest rates and those of the Euro participants will be less than it is with regard to the mark and German rates," Jacobsen said.
Danish exporters say the crown is already too strong against foreign currencies, a fact widely blamed for the virtual collapse of the shipbuilding industry.
"We are strongly pro-EMU, all our companies are strongly positive for it," Confederation of Danish Industry official Richard Larsen told Reuters.

Jacobsen said a common European currency would reduce opportunities for foreign exchange speculation, encouraging a flow of speculative capital to Denmark, where the economy is strong but the currency and interest rates would float against the Euro structure.

Unibank's Ellen Ploeger agreed in principle with Jacobsen but said the type of monetary arrangement between the European central bank and countries outside the Euro currency zone would be a crucial factor.
Economy Minister Marianne Jelved has spoken of the need for the closest possible ties between the crown and the Euro.

"If Denmark is closely linked to the Euro and agrees a pledge of mutual assistance with the European central bank then I would agree that the yield gap would narrow as we would have a guarantee of support for the crown," Ploeger told Berlingske. --Steve Weizman, Copenhagen newsroom +45 33969650
